objective: Facilitating conflict management: identifying a conflict's root cause and level, and promoting a collaborative resolution approach
secondaryObjectives: Empowering teams: building trust and transparent communication, coaching and mentoring, and applying emotional intelligence to resolve conflict and support the team

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) Examination Content Outline (March 2026): Mindset 28%, Leadership 25%, Product 19%, Delivery 28%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of PMI's PDF. Relevant text: Domain IV Task 1 'Seek early feedback' ('Deliver work in small increments'; 'Collect and incorporate stakeholders' feedback on a regular basis'); Task 3 'Manage impediments and risk' ('Proactively identify risks and impediments'; 'Prioritize impediment removal and risk mitigation activities'); Domain I Task 7 'Embrace Change' ('Embrace process adaptation by responding to changing requirements and priorities'; 'Adapt to product needs based on the learning and feedback'). The objective wording here is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's sprint-release-before-review-pmiacp (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The company, the product, the team and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the agile coach for a team at Seabright Travel, a fictional travel company. Developers and test specialists have started blaming each other: testers say code arrives untested on the last day; developers say testers block releases.
handover: Testing happens in the last two days of each iteration.
Last retrospective ended with raised voices.
howItWorks: The board shows the Sprint's commitments, the work, the impediments, the people's support and the Scrum events.
Move on a day at a time. A decision comes to you at each Daily Scrum; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Day 2: the lead tester hears of it and asks to leave the team; testing knowledge leaves with her.
Day 3: developers test superficially to meet the rule; a payment bug ships.
Day 4: a tester spots a risk but says nothing for fear of 'breaking the agreement'; it reaches production.

effects.log: Day 1: two people refuse to pair.
Day 3: a week after the agreement.

levelPrompt.title: How serious is this?
levelPrompt.context: It is moving from problem-solving to blame between two groups.

choices.label: Name it as a growing conflict between groups over a broken workflow, not personalities; plan a facilitated session focused on the shared problem

effects.log: You frame the conflict around the workflow.

choices.feedback: Identifying the level and root cause points the resolution at the process, not at people.

choices.label: Let it settle by itself over the iteration
choices.feedback: Conflicts at the blame stage tend to escalate when ignored.

choices.label: Tell the manager the lead tester is the problem
choices.feedback: Personalizing a process conflict escalates it and destroys trust.

choices.label: Facilitate: shared goal first, the flow data on the wall, both sides propose changes; they agree testers join refinement and work is tested as each story finishes

effects.log: The team agrees its own changes.

choices.feedback: Collaboration addresses both sides' interests and gives the team ownership of the fix.

choices.label: Split the difference: testing starts on day 7 instead of day 9
choices.feedback: Better, but nobody's real interest is met and stories still flood late.

choices.label: Decide for them: developers must test their own code, testers only sign off
choices.feedback: Forcing a solution builds resentment and removes the testers' expertise.

followPrompt.title: Making it stick
followPrompt.context: The new agreement is a week old.

choices.label: Put the agreement on the board, and at the retrospective let the team inspect the flow data and adjust; coach the two people who clashed one to one

effects.log: The team inspects and adjusts its agreement.

choices.feedback: Transparency and inspection let the team keep improving; coaching rebuilds trust.

choices.label: Assume it's fixed
choices.feedback: Without inspection, old habits come back.

choices.label: Warn that anyone breaking the agreement will be reported
choices.feedback: Threats replace trust with fear; people stop raising problems.

reflection.question: Write your coaching notes: what the conflict was really about, how it was resolved, and how it will be kept resolved.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: A group conflict at the blame stage caused by end-of-iteration testing.
parts.modelAnswer: It was a workflow conflict: work flooded testing on the last two days, and both groups blamed each other.

parts.label: Resolution
parts.criteria: Facilitated collaboration; testers in refinement; test as stories finish; inspected at retrospectives.
parts.modelAnswer: In a facilitated session the team agreed testers join refinement and stories are tested as they finish; the retrospective inspects it.

scoring.modelReasoning: Conflict management starts with the conflict's level (from a problem to solve, through disagreement, to contest and crusade) and its root cause, here a workflow that pushed all testing to the end. Collaborative resolution, facilitated with data and owned by the team, addresses both sides' interests; forcing or blaming escalates. Follow-up comes through transparency, the team's own retrospectives and coaching.
